newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium stocks to fall dramatically - T. Hoare.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium stocks to fall dramatically - T. Hoare.

text.p: Aluminium inventories will fall dramatically to the equivalent of 2.4 weeks of Western demand by 2000 from this year's 7.8 weeks if idled capacity remains off-stream, broker T. Hoare said in a research report.
Copper will move in the opposite direction, however, with inventories rising to 29.5 weeks of demand from an estimated 11.6 in 1997 as new mines come on stream, analyst Rhona O'Connell said.
The scenario for aluminium assumed that one million tonnes of production capacity idled in line with the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) among producing nations would remain off-stream.
"If there were no restarts from the sidelined capacity then aluminium inventories would be at perilously low levels by the end of the decade," O'Connell said.
But as prices climbed from an estimated 7.8 cents per lb ($1,631 per tonne) this year, producers would reactivate output when they reached a "reasonable" price, she added.

"Anecdotal evidence suggests that a 'reasonable' price in this context is closer to 90 cents ($1,984) than 80 cents ($1,764), although some may be tempted into the fray at slightly lower levels," the report said.
O'Connell expected prices to rise to an average 80 cents next year and 85 cents ($1,874) in 1999 and 2000.
As copper inventories built up, prices would slide from 106 cents ($2,337) estimated for this year to 80 cents ($1,764) in 2000.

There were more than 100 new greenfield or expansion projects expected between the start of 1997 and the end of 2000, with almost four million tonnes of potential fresh capacity, not taking into account any closures.
At least a quarter of the fresh output would be from the SX-EW process which normally had cash costs in the 40 cents region ($882), the report said.

"The vast amount (of production) scheduled to come on stream will eventually smother the market and force prices closer to production costs, undermining the viability of high-cost producers," O'Connell said.
Nickel inventories were also expected to balloon, from 7.4 weeks of demand this year to 24.7 weeks in 2000.
Prices were seen declining from 330 cents ($7,275) this year to 275 cents ($6,063) by 2000.

"The nickel producers should enjoy one more bout of strength as the stainless steel market picks up and returns to demand for primary metal, having been working off scrap stainless supply," the report said.
As the massive Voisey's Bay project geared up and laterite producers strove to come on stream, the market would see a tussle for market share, it added.
